title: Looking for honest feedback on my project — what’s your first impression?
author: abner-ruza
selftext:
Hey everyone! I’m working on a project and put together this short video to get some early feedback.

I’d love to hear your honest first impressions. Does it look interesting? What catches your attention, and what feels confusing or could be improved?

It’s still a work in progress, so I’m mainly trying to understand what resonates with people and what needs more work. Critical feedback is welcome!

Thanks for taking a look!

comments.author: FrankenChocula
comments.body: Cool graphics.  No gameplay so got bored after about 8 seconds.  Needs something to actually do.  (And when implementing, ensure the character can move fast enough to make it fun.)  Good luck!

replies.author: abner-ruza
replies.body: Thanks for the honest feedback! This is mostly an experiment to see how far I can take it, so I’ve been focusing on the visuals so far. Fair point about the gameplay and movement speed though — I’ll keep that in mind as I build it out. Appreciate you checking it out!

replies.author: abner-ruza
replies.body:
Haha I’m figuring a lot of this out with AI too, so don’t assume I’m some Godot expert... The terrain is generated through code, then I tweak the layout and visuals. Getting it to look like this took a lot of back and forth.

I actually like the base setup in yours! What you’re seeing in my video is the part I’ve spent most of my time on, so it’s a bit of an unfair comparison.

When generating assets, keep giving it those references and ask for individual pieces with the same palette, perspective, and lighting. Then check them together in Godot — something can look great on its own and still feel out of place in the scene.

comments.author: Elegant_Tech
comments.body: Great visuals! So I guess the question is do you have a fun game that you built first? Or have you been focused on visuals and still need to design the game? Most people tend to use placeholder stub art trying to make a fun game first. Nice thing is you do have a pipeline for great graphics to come back to as you build out the game if you haven't yet.

replies.author: abner-ruza
replies.body:
Thanks! You guessed right — I’ve been focusing on the visuals so far. This started as an experiment to see how far I could take the atmosphere and world, rather than with a finished gameplay idea.

I agree that looking good and being fun to play are different challenges. Figuring out what would make exploring this world enjoyable is the next step. And yeah, having this visual pipeline in place should help a lot as I build on it. Appreciate the thoughtful feedback!

comments.author: SwoopsMackenzie
comments.body: Gorgeous. Any tips you can share for art/rendering?

replies.author: abner-ruza
replies.body:
Thanks! What helped most was keeping a consistent palette and using the same visual references across the assets, including the AI-generated textures.  
  
On the rendering side, the terrain uses continuous textures with irregular coastlines and cliff edges. Patches of grass, exposed soil, and small stones help break up repetition. Soft contact shadows ground the plants and rocks, while shared lighting ties everything together. Subtle wind and water movement add a lot to the atmosphere too.

Lots of small adjustments rather than one magic trick!

The slow walk was meant to feel cautious, but a few people have mentioned it now, so it needs tweaking. It’s still an early tech demo. the bigger goal is to make exploring another planet feel believable, strange, and a little terrifying.

comments.author: Briskfall
comments.body:
Night time looks pretty and atmospheric -- really nice! (though I think that it would look nicer if the glow for the character wasn't as obvious and place it like as a lamp or smth, and use edge light to enhance the whole atmosphere). 8.5/10

Daytime gives me the jeebies. (if that's intentional) I do not want to spend longer than 5 seconds still on that spot! But it still looks polished. 6/10

GUI looks like placeholder. Looks like a webapp and doesn't really scream "game." Killed a bit some of my interest. 4/10

replies.author: abner-ruza
replies.body:
Thanks for breaking it down! Putting the light on the suit as an actual lamp makes a lot of sense. I like the edge lighting suggestion too.

And haha, a little uneasy is definitely what I’m going for! You’ve just landed on Proxima b and have no idea what’s safe around you. Hopefully I can make you curious enough to stay longer than five seconds ...

Fair point on the UI. It’s mostly controls for testing the environment right now, and it needs a proper design as the game takes shape. Glad the nighttime atmosphere worked for you!

comments.author: BreakfastHuman5937

I like the vibrant colors. More interesting than the typical desolate planet - cool vibe.  
  
If you're asking for a critical judgement: above all the UI elements scream AI html demo to me. I struggle with that myself so I'm not one to offer any guidance on how to improve it.

It's hard to grade anything beyond that because idk what the gameplay loop is, but it looks cool so far.

replies.author: abner-ruza
replies.body:
Thanks! That’s what I was hoping for with the colors. You’re a human explorer arriving on Proxima b, and I wanted it to feel strange and alive, somewhere you’d want to explore but wouldn’t know what’s safe to touch.

And haha, fair call on the UI. A lot of those controls are there so I can test lighting and environmental effects, but they definitely need a rethink for the game.

It’s mostly a tech demo right now, so the gameplay loop is still taking shape. I have a much bigger idea for it, but making the exploration actually fun is the part I still need to prove.

replies.author: Maple-Syrup89
replies.body:
But this clearly isn't a 1 shot. AI just typing the code of a shader is not unique - what the human asks for to direct an guide it 20 times until its perfect is. 

One example - I build tools for my games. I have over 450 independent controls to adjust every single aspect of every element in the game, from physics, to look and feel, every single tuning detail is down to my choice. And I have a very small vertical slice of my game. I expect to have fine tuned 2000+ elements by the time I am even close to a shareable state. 

None of that is AI designing my game. It's AI typing code for me and helping with automated tests.

replies.author: abner-ruza
replies.body:
That's exactly what I'm doing right now. It's several techniques combined.  
I'm asking the AI ​​to create editing and terrain creation tools. Procedural generation in the editor so I can manually optimize; color filters, etc. Lots of manual settings too. I believe the AI ​​doesn't have the Feeling yet.
